title: Jamesport Site
summary: The Jamesport Site is an Orient Period (1,000-1,300 BC) ceremonial burial ground. Archaeological work documented red ochre, burial offerings, and deliberately broken stone vessels associated with ceremonial practice. Riverhead Town purchased the land in 2017 because of its cultural significance and the need for protection.

why_this_matters: Containing ceremonial offerings like intentionally "killed" steatite bowls and caches of red ochre, the Jamesport Site provides remarkable insight into the deep spiritual practices of Long Island's early inhabitants. Riverhead Town's 2017 purchase of the property to prevent development demonstrates a growing, vital commitment by local municipalities to respectfully preserve the few remaining sacred Indigenous burial grounds.
preservation_content: Jamesport is a sacred burial landscape requiring care and protection. Its story centers preservation, Native community advocacy, and respect. Exact coordinates, feature locations, and directions to burial places are not appropriate for display; only reviewed, general civic or preservation context is used.
excavation_content:
The Jamesport Site has been described as a transitional site, as it features both a clay and soapstone vessel fragments. The one clay vessel, done in ceramic, was a precise copy of the soapstone vessels in the same site. A low, elongated form, with a lug on each end. It is not, however, soapstone-tempered, and the Orient area is beyond the geographic range of Sheldon Island soapstone-tempered pottery. Ninety percent of the sherds of this clay vessel were high in the pit fill; none of it was on the floor with the grave caches, killed soapstone pots, and deposits of ochre. It would appear that it was late in the culture there. There was a proportion of one clay vessel to sixty soapstone vessels in that component. There were also several arrow points, evidently of later types than those in the two components in Orient, but of Early Woodland forms. Broad spearheads were found in this grave pit, some of them intentionally broken.

We have referred to these large blades as knives. It is noteworthy, perhaps, to record that only one large or broad blade was in a cache. One spear may have been in single ownership instead of one knife; we have conjectured, that one knife or one spear was all that one person required.

We have assumed that a cache represented the possessions of one individual interment. All large soapstone pottery vessels apparently were in family or group usage, as they were broken and scattered in association with human bone fragments throughout the floor of the big grave pits, commonly in disregard of the caches. The exception were a few small soapstone bowls, which were probably personal pieces placed u-right in the center of the caches with their objects arranged around them. These cached pots were not cracked up like the larger ones, but a whole had been punched through the bottom, always inward from the outside. No plug from the bottom of these small killed pots has been recovered. They were destroyed or carried away. Similarly killed soapstone pots have been found in the Susquehanna Valley, but they have not been found in place, but were washed out of floodplains.

Study of the arrangement of cached goods and placement of broken soapstone vessels in the Orient is extremely interesting. These traits will not be described here. [1. Truex, J. E. (1981). The Second coastal archaeology reader: 1900 to the present. Stony Brook, NY: Suffolk County Archaeological Association. pp. 62]
